deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous page Gauss states his 'Grundgesetz' of July 1835 for two moving charges, F = ee'/r^2 {1 + k(|v_rel|^2 - 3/2 (dr/dt)^2)}. On this page he starts from the macroscopic law for current elements: Ampère's elementary force. He then converts it, for a closed second circuit, into a simpler equivalent form. The next page finishes that conversion and interprets it back in terms of the charge law.

(1) Ampère's law in Gauss's angle convention. Let P = (x,y,z) lie in the first current and P' = (x',y',z') in the second, with r = |PP'|. ds and ds' are the current elements starting at P and P'. Define:
- u = angle(ds, ds');
- q = angle(ds, PP');
- q' = angle(ds', P'P).
Dropping the current-intensity factors, the mutual attraction is F = ds ds' (cos u + 3/2 cos q cos q')/r^2.
In Ampère's usual convention both angles are measured from the same vector r, giving the repulsion form (ds ds'/r^2)(cos ε - 3/2 cos θ cos θ'). Gauss measures q' from P'P = -r, so cos q' = -cos θ'. His attraction formula is therefore exactly Ampère's law (Ampère's constant k = -1/2).

(2) Special frame. Gauss puts dx = dy = 0, i.e. ds lies along the z-axis. [Mine: he tacitly takes ds = +dz.] Then:
- cos u = dz'/ds';
- cos q = (z'-z)/r;
- cos q' = [(x-x')dx' + (y-y')dy' + (z-z')dz']/(r ds') = -dr/ds', where dr is the change of r as P' moves along ds' with P fixed.
Hence F = ds dz'/r^2 - (3/2)((z'-z)/r^3) ds ds' (dr/ds'). This matches the manuscript; the overwritten 'ds.d s'' is just ds ds'.

(3) Components. The attraction on ds points along PP', unit vector (x'-x, y'-y, z'-z)/r. Multiplying out gives
F_i = ds{(x_i'-x_i) dz'/r^3 - 3(x_i'-x_i)(z'-z) dr/(2r^4)}, for i = x, y, z.
This is exactly as written.

(4) Exact-differential trick. Gauss adds -ds d[(x_i'-x_i)(z'-z)/(2r^3)], where d is the differential along the second circuit. Its integral around a closed current ds' vanishes, so the total force of a closed circuit on ds is unchanged. Hence the remark '…was insofern ds' Element eines geschlossenen Stromes ist, erlaubt ist'.
[Mine:] d[(x'-x)(z'-z)/(2r^3)] = [(z'-z)dx' + (x'-x)dz']/(2r^3) - 3(x'-x)(z'-z)dr/(2r^4). Subtracting it from (3) gives the next page's result:
F_i = ds[(x_i'-x_i)dz' - (z'-z)dx_i']/(2r^3).
The z-component vanishes.

(5) Vector form [mine]. With R = P'-P this reads dF = (1/(2r^3))[R (ds·ds') - ds'(ds·R)] = -(1/(2r^3)) ds×(ds'×R). This is the Grassmann / Biot–Savart (Lorentz-type) element force. So the page proves that, for a closed acting circuit, Ampère's element force can be replaced by Grassmann's.
The next page then reads this as:
- a force ds ds' cos u/(2r^2) along PP';
- a force -ds ds' cos q/(2r^2) parallel to ds';
- an addable term +ds ds' cos q'/(2r^2) along ds.
He explains these via the velocity-dependent charge law.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. All of the following were checked symbolically: the reduction in the frame dx=dy=0, the components, and the exact differential.
Implicit, not an error: setting dx=dy=0 also tacitly takes ds = +dz (orientation of the z-axis along the current).

Implicit, not an error: dr and d(...) mean differentials along the second circuit with P held fixed. The exact differentials added in (4) are legitimate only for the total force of a closed circuit ds'. They change the force between individual element pairs.

Consequence for the next page: there the claim that ds' then feels exactly opposite forces is not justified by this transformation alone. The modified element force no longer satisfies action = reaction pairwise; that holds only when the ds-circuit is also closed. This is a point to flag, not an error on this page.

results.what: Ampère's elementary force between current elements, written as attraction ds ds'(cos u + 3/2 cos q cos q')/r^2 with q' measured from P'P
For a closed acting circuit, Ampère's force on an element equals ds·[R dz' - (z'-z) ds']/(2r^3), i.e. -(1/2r^3) ds×(ds'×R), obtained by adding exact differentials d[(x_i'-x_i)(z'-z)/(2r^3)]
results.modern_name: Equivalence of the Ampère and Grassmann (Biot–Savart/Lorentz) element forces for closed circuits
results.usually_credited_to: H. Grassmann 1845 (Grassmann's force law); the equivalence was later discussed by Maxwell (Treatise, 1873)

results.what: Context: Gauss's July 1835 velocity-dependent charge law F = ee'/r^2[1 + k(v^2 - 3/2 ṙ^2)] used as the source of the current-element law
results.modern_name: Gauss's electrodynamic law (precursor of Weber's 1846 law)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, published in Werke V, 1867; discussed by Maxwell, Treatise Art. 851)

deep.surprise_reason: The page belongs to Gauss's well-known 1835 'Grundgesetz' notes, published in Werke V pp. 616ff (the marginal 'p 617' refers to that printing). Its mathematical content is a correct reduction of Ampère's law, showing that for closed circuits it is equivalent to the Grassmann/Biot–Savart element force. This anticipates Grassmann (1845), but it has been in print since 1867 and is known to historians of electrodynamics. It is therefore a notable but documented detail, not a new attribution.

checkable.sympy: x,y,z,xp,yp,zp,dxp,dyp,dzp=symbols('x y z xp yp zp dxp dyp dzp',real=True); r=sqrt((xp-x)**2+(yp-y)**2+(zp-z)**2); dr=((xp-x)*dxp+(yp-y)*dyp+(zp-z)*dzp)/r; dsp=sqrt(dxp**2+dyp**2+dzp**2); simplify(((x-xp)*dxp+(y-yp)*dyp+(z-zp)*dzp)/(r*dsp) + dr/dsp) == 0
checkable.asserts: cos q' = -dr/ds' when q' is measured from ds' to P'P
With ds = dz (dx=dy=0), Ampère's force per ds equals dz'/r^2 - 3/2 (z'-z)/r^3 dr, as on the page
Adding -d[(x'-x)(z'-z)/(2r^3)] turns the x-component into ((x'-x)dz' - (z'-z)dx')/(2r^3), as on the next page
The z-component becomes identically zero after adding the exact differential

checkable.sympy: R=Matrix([xp-x,yp-y,zp-z]); a=Matrix([0,0,1]); b=Matrix([dxp,dyp,dzp]); simplify((R*a.dot(b) - b*a.dot(R)) + a.cross(b.cross(R))) == zeros(3,1)
checkable.asserts: The resulting force has vector form -(1/(2r^3)) ds×(ds'×R), i.e. Grassmann's element force

transcription_corrections: Header 'X p 617' is most likely 'V p 617' (or the same 'I p 61x' marker as the previous page). It refers to the printed page in Gauss's Werke Bd. V, p. 617.
'ds.d[-s-]{+s+}'' should read simply 'ds.ds'' (an overwritten s), i.e. -3/2 (z'-z)/r^3 · ds·ds'·(dr/ds').
'Es sein P und P'': the first P is written over another letter; read 'Es seien P und P''.
A stray left parenthesis/bracket stands in the margin before the displayed Ampère formula; it is not part of the formula.
